cards.title: Why the welcome flow exists: email as the cheap way across the trust threshold
cards.summary: Use the welcome flow to send trust-building content at scale, because paid traffic alone makes a first-time buyer too expensive.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much budget and effort to put into the post-signup welcome flow versus buying more ad impressions.
steps: Start from the source's funnel math: only a small share of site traffic (he cites ~2%) is ready to buy on the first visit; the rest arrive with objections about brand legitimacy, product quality and price. Those objections cannot be answered by one ad, so buyers need repeated exposure — the source calls this crossing the 'trust threshold'.

Recognise that the only other channel that reaches people daily at low marginal cost is email — the source cites 4B+ global email users, 90%+ of the US population checking email daily, and average $44 returned per $1 spent on email versus roughly $2 per $1 on paid ads. Treat those ratios as the source's cited industry averages, not guaranteed results.

Apply to your store: for each objection on your PDP (does this work, is this brand real, is it worth the price), assign at least one email in the flow that answers it, so paid spend does not have to be repeated to convince the same person.
Keep the objective in mind for measurement: the welcome flow's job is partly immediate conversion and partly priming future purchases, so judging it only by its own revenue understates its value.
caveats: ROAS and percentage figures are the source's cited averages; your niche, price point and traffic source will differ.
Email only works if you are actually capturing addresses — without a popup or lead magnet, the flow has nobody to send to.

cards.title: Set the welcome flow length and goal by price point and buying cycle
cards.summary: Run the welcome sequence over 7-14 days for typical AOV, stretching to months for high-ticket products with long consideration.
cards.use_when: Scoping how many emails and how many days your welcome/onboarding flow should cover before you write it.
steps: Default to a 7-14 day window for a normal AOV store — the source's typical recommendation.
If AOV is very high (he gives the example of a ~$5,000 product), extend the flow well beyond that, potentially over two months, because the buying decision itself takes longer.

Define two outcomes you are designing for: (a) converting the curious signups who would otherwise bounce, and (b) priming future customers by addressing objections up front. Priming shows up later, e.g. the source claims a campaign sent to a primed list can produce a far larger revenue day ($75k vs $5k in his illustrative example) — treat that as illustration, not a benchmark.
Plan the flow as separate, spread-out emails rather than a couple of dense ones, and pick an email count that matches the length of the consideration window.
caveats: The 7-14 day range and two-month high-ticket example are the source's heuristics, not tested universals.
The revenue comparison used to illustrate priming is an anecdote; do not promise it internally as a forecast.

cards.title: Split dense welcome emails into short, skimmable, spread-out messages
cards.summary: Fix short-but-crammed welcome flows by cutting information per email and spreading it across more emails.
cards.use_when: Auditing an existing welcome flow that crams brand story, bestsellers, FAQ and offer into 2-3 long emails.
steps: Accept the skim reality: the source states customers spend at most roughly 5-7 seconds on an email, so the whole flow's information cannot live in two walls of text.
Keep body copy minimal — the source calls anything over about 100 words 'too much' for these emails. Use short headlines and one idea per email.
Structure every email so the reader can get the point in about three seconds: clear headline, one supporting proof or claim, discount reminder if one exists, and a button.
Place a button near the top of every email so nobody has to scroll to act, and repeat a button at the bottom for readers who reach the end.

Assign one job per email across the sequence (intro + incentive, brand story, bestseller, offer reminder, us-vs-them, social proof, last chance, founder note) rather than duplicating everything everywhere.
caveats: The 100-word and 5-7 second figures are the source's rules of thumb for ecommerce promo email, not formal research.
Short emails do not mean skipping the offer reminder — the source specifically criticises welcome emails that never restate the discount.

cards.title: Email 1: deliver the incentive and prove legitimacy in the first screen
cards.summary: Open the welcome flow with a fast, purpose-built email that hands over the discount and gives enough proof to click now.
cards.use_when: Writing or rewriting the first email a new subscriber receives after opting in.
steps: Put the welcome and the discount at the very top with the incentive code visible and a shop-now button above the fold, so the discount-only crowd can convert without scrolling.
Add a short brand message headline (the source's example uses two words carrying the brand's positioning) so skimmers absorb what you stand for without reading a paragraph.
Include one short social proof element and one or two differentiators (USPs), then the discount and another button.
Show bestsellers below so people who do not know what to buy have a default choice, not a blank stare at your homepage.
Close with a bottom button — the source notes most people will not scroll back up to find a top button if they end up at the base of the email.
caveats: Design should be simple and clean; heavy layouts compete with the one action you want.
Only discount-led lead capture suits this email; if your opt-in is a lead magnet or content offer, deliver that instead.

cards.title: Email 2: put a face to the brand to convert skeptical new signups
cards.summary: Use the brand-story email to humanise the store and address the 'who are these people, are they real' objection.
cards.use_when: Building the second email in the welcome flow for a store that customers find through ads and don't recognise.
steps: Assume the reason they have not purchased yet is partly that you are a faceless brand they stumbled on in an ad; the email's job is to make you feel like a real small company with a mission.
Include a founding story in about two sentences, the mission, and — critically — a real face (photo of founders or maker), plus the reason the brand was started.
State one or two differentiators (ingredients, process, sourcing) so the story is not only emotional but informative.
Remind them of the discount above the button; include the button and a brand-aesthetic image.
Do not expect this email to be a big revenue driver — the source says it will make some sales, but its real value is priming and trust building for later purchases.
caveats: A fabricated or stock 'founder' image undermines the trust the email is meant to build.
Emotional storytelling still needs factual product claims to satisfy skeptical buyers.

cards.title: Email 3: use a bestseller email to collapse choice paralysis
cards.summary: Spotlight one or a few bestsellers with reasons, so undecided buyers don't have to choose between your whole catalogue.
cards.use_when: Designing the mid-flow email for a store with a large catalogue where new subscribers don't know what to buy.
steps: Apply the source's observation that customers want choices but hate making them — so make the decision for them by featuring one or a few bestsellers rather than the full range.

Give the bestseller a reason: not just the product name but specific, brief qualities (the example uses protein, fibre, prebiotics, plant ingredients), so the qualities you praise transfer to how the brand is perceived.
Use one or two words or short bullets per point rather than sentences; keep proof concrete, not essay-length.
Adapt the layout to a specific hero product, e.g. one shirt or one flavour, while keeping the same structure of headline, hero image, reasons, discount, buttons.
Close with a discount reminder and a button, ideally with a button near the top as well.
caveats: The 'wants choices but hates choosing' idea is the source's framing of consumer psychology, not a tested law.
Featuring a product that is actually out of stock or barely stocked will burn the trust this email builds.

cards.title: Email 4: add urgency plus risk reversal to push the fence-sitters
cards.summary: Turn the coupon reminder into a decision email by combining time pressure, testimonials and guarantees.
cards.use_when: Writing the offer-reminder email mid-flow when subscribers are informed but still not purchasing.
steps: Write a headline that addresses the discount directly and states the code is expiring — the source's example pairs 'friendly reminder that your discount code is expiring' with 'we don't offer discounts often', which creates urgency and positions the brand as non-discount.

Add risk reversals that answer the remaining purchase objections: free shipping, satisfaction guarantee, easy/free returns. The source flags the absence of risk reversals as the main improvement available in this kind of email.
Use testimonials for trust, and consider pairing testimonials with individual products plus their discounts, so proof and offer sit together.
Make the button large and unmistakable so clicking is trivially easy on mobile; the source argues an oversized button drives a very high click rate.
Include a bottom link to browse the whole catalogue for readers who did not like the featured products.
caveats: Frequent fake urgency erodes credibility — only claim expirations you will actually enforce.
The 'we don't offer discounts often' line only works if it is true for your brand.

cards.title: Email 5: answer 'why you instead of the competitor' head-on
cards.summary: Use a direct comparison email to let shoppers evaluate you against alternatives and conclude you win.
cards.use_when: Building the comparison email for a crowded niche where buyers are weighing several similar brands.
steps: Lead with the elephant in the room: in most niches there are thousands of alternatives, so state why someone should pick you.

Use a short comparison table or list with brief 1-3 word points (the source's example contrasts customisation vs non-customisable, simple ordering vs complicated ordering, thoughtful gifting vs standard delivery). Keep it fast to scan.
Follow the comparison with one expanded differentiator and an emotional benefit — the source's example describes what a delivered gourmet meal does for a corporate event or anniversary.
Add a short testimonial for proof, then the discount and a shop-now button — the source also recommends a discount banner at the top of the email.
Keep claims factual and comparable; you are giving shoppers the facts so they can choose, which is what the source argues makes the decision easy.
caveats: Naming competitors invites regulatory and legal risk in some markets — check the rules before comparing by brand name.
Overstated comparison points that customers can verify as false destroy the trust the rest of the flow built.

cards.title: Email 6: dedicate a whole email to social proof
cards.summary: Use one email purely for testimonials, reviews and media mentions to certify that your brand and products are legitimate.
cards.use_when: Building the trust email in the welcome flow, especially for new or unfamiliar brands.
steps: Fill the email almost entirely with proof: customer testimonials, verified reviews, review counts and ratings, media features. The source argues that even someone who only sees the subject line learns you are confident enough to stand behind your product.

Visualise the rating distribution rather than just citing an average, and label reviews as verified — the source says his team tested that adding 'verified' next to a buyer's name improves conversions.
Put a strong testimonial high in the email so it is visible on open, then add further reviews or a rating graphic.
Include risk-reversal icons (secure payment, fast and free shipping, quality guarantee) and a button at the bottom for readers who are now in a buying mood.
Use this email to answer the 'will this product actually work for me' objection, which is a reason people delay, not a reason they buy immediately.
caveats: The claim that 'verified' next to a review lifts conversion is from the source's own testing, not a published benchmark.
Do not invent or aggregate reviews you cannot verify — unverifiable proof is more damaging than none.

cards.title: Emails 7-8: close with hard urgency, then a founder's personal note
cards.summary: Finish the flow with a last-chance discount email followed by a plain-text founder message extending the offer and inviting replies.
cards.use_when: Writing the final two emails of a welcome flow, for subscribers who have received the whole sequence without buying.
steps: For email 7, keep it extremely simple: 'last chance' headline, product graphic, clear discount code, extreme urgency copy (the source's example ends the phrase with 'expires forever'), plus social proof icons and one big button.

For email 8, switch to a plain text-based message from the founder: brief intro, reminder that the welcome discount was not used, an extension for one more day, a single shop-now link, and an invitation to reply with questions.

Keep the text email to one action so there is nothing else to do but click; the source argues this simplicity, plus the personal tone, makes text-based founder emails among the highest-performing emails in the sequence.
Use the final email to surface an objection: invite replies and commit to a response time, so anyone stuck on a question can get it answered and then buy.
caveats: Treat the source's claim that text-based personal emails are top performers as his experience, not a universal result.
Only extend the discount if you intend to honour it; repeat extensions train subscribers to wait.

cards.title: Configure the Clavio trigger and filter so buyers drop out of the flow
cards.summary: Install the welcome flow with a signup trigger and a zero-purchases filter so existing and new buyers don't keep receiving sales emails.
cards.use_when: Setting up or auditing the automation behind your welcome/onboarding email sequence.
steps: Set the trigger to the specific list subscribers join from your popup (the source's example uses subscription to the 'newsletter' list), matching whatever your opt-in form actually adds people to.
Add a flow filter set to 'placed order zero times since starting this flow' so a purchase removes the person from the sequence.
Optionally use 'zero times over all time' if you want to be certain past purchasers never enter the flow; the source notes this as a more conservative option.
Verify the settings in your own platform's current interface, since trigger and filter naming changes between versions and tools.
Recheck the filter whenever you add a new popup, form or list, because a mismatched trigger means the flow silently never fires.
caveats: The described Clavio trigger/filter wording is from the source's setup and may not match the current UI exactly.
If your store sells high-frequency consumables, excluding all past purchasers may be wrong — decide based on whether the flow is genuinely welcome-only.

cards.title: Give the welcome flow a target conversion rate and a testing loop
cards.summary: Judge and improve the flow against a realistic conversion band, then compound gains with continuous A/B tests.
cards.use_when: Reviewing welcome flow performance or deciding whether to invest in optimisation work.
steps: Set expectations with the source's heuristic: a 10% conversion rate from the welcome flow is his stated gold standard, and 20% would be considered very strong. Do not treat these as guaranteed outcomes.
Accept that even at the gold standard, roughly 90% will not buy — so the flow's other job (priming) must continue through the rest of your email programme.

A/B test the specific elements the source prioritises: subject lines and preview text, the offer structure (e.g. $10 off vs 10% off vs free shipping vs a free item with first order), which products are featured, and text-based versus graphic-based versions of individual emails.
Also test linking to specific products versus linking to collections.
In Clavio, the source prefers running the split with a conditional split because the numbers are easier to read; confirm the current split test tooling in your platform.
Track small gains as compounding: his illustrative example is a store doing 100k/month with 10k from the flow, where a monthly 10% improvement adds ~1k in the first month and compounds thereafter.
caveats: 10% and 20% are the source's stated targets for welcome flows, not universal benchmarks.
The compounding arithmetic is an illustration, not a forecast; actual gains depend on traffic and repeatability.

cards.title: Reuse winning campaigns as welcome-flow emails to save build time
cards.summary: Monitor your regular campaigns and insert proven ones into the welcome flow with a first-order code added.
cards.use_when: Optimising the welcome flow when you have limited time to write new emails.
steps: Send 3-4 campaigns per week to your list, mostly non-promotional, and watch which angles outperform.

When a campaign clearly crushes, adapt it for the flow: add a line such as 'use code XYZ for XYZ off your first order' and insert it into the sequence, or replace the weakest-performing welcome email.
Use this to avoid building net-new emails while still refreshing the flow's content.

Try campaign angles the source names as working well in welcome flows: myths vs facts in your industry, blog promotion, a specific product spotlight, a testimonial spotlight, a customer story, and product restock announcements.
Keep the flow's core structure (intro, story, bestseller, urgency, proof, last chance) even as individual emails are swapped.
caveats: Check the swapped email still fits the sequence logic and does not repeat what another email already says.
Campaigns written for existing subscribers may assume context a new subscriber lacks; adjust the copy accordingly.
